title: Which women wrote the unsigned stories in nineteenth-century newspapers?
short: A newspaper might print a novel one chapter at a time and drop the byline when it reprinted it. Following the chapters could restore a writer’s name and career.
matters: Newspapers in different countries carried the same stories under different titles. A signed instalment in one town can supply the credit missing from an entire run elsewhere. Connecting several such runs could show a woman earning a living from fiction well beyond the readership of any book published under her name.
stuck: A pen name could belong to more than one writer. Editors shortened stories and syndicates distributed the same version to many papers. A resemblance in writing style cannot by itself supply an author’s identity or gender.
solved: Link an unsigned serial to a named writer through independent evidence such as a copyright registration, a publisher’s payment or a signed version with a documented attribution. Measure mistaken identifications on known writers before proposing names for unknown ones.
approach: Trace successive instalments in Chronicling America, Trove and Gallica through changes of title, byline and language. Count reprints of a common source together.
Fix the authorship test in advance using signed serials, including writers outside the candidate set. Test it on withheld works and report false matches by language and genre.
Follow promising matches into copyright ledgers, correspondence, syndicate notices and obituaries. Document the evidence that a pseudonym belonged to a particular person.

needs.ask: Test whether style comparisons distinguish authors after accounting for genre, translation and the wording of shared reprints.
